@graph.headline: Charitable Lead Trusts and Digital Assets: Why the Section 170(e)(1)(A) Basis Limitation Does Not Reach a Charitable Lead Interest, Where the One-Year Holding Period Still Bites, and How Section 7520 Makes the Appraisal the Whole Deduction
@graph.description: An analysis of charitable lead trusts funded with cryptocurrency, NFTs, and other digital assets. Explains how IRC Section 170(e)(1)(A) reduces a property contribution by the gain that would not have been long-term capital gain; why 26 CFR Section 1.170A-4(a) confines that reduction to interests described in Section 1.170A-6(b) and Section 1.170A-7(b); why Section 1.170A-4(b)(1) expressly excludes an income interest allowed under Section 170(f)(2)(B) from the definition of ordinary income property; how Section 170(f)(2)(B) makes a guaranteed annuity or fixed-percentage unitrust interest a condition of deductibility; how grantor and non-grantor status divides the Section 170 deduction from the Section 642(c) trust deduction; how Section 7520(a) builds the rate from 120 percent of the applicable federal midterm rate, why the October 2026 rate is 5.6 percent under Rev. Rul. 2026-19, and why a higher rate lowers the present value of a fixed annuity; the three dates that must align between the contribution, the Section 7520 valuation date, and the appraisal's date of value; why a charitable lead unitrust requires annual revaluation of corpus while a charitable lead annuity trust does not; where the one-year holding period still determines character at the trust level on sale and on in-kind annuity satisfaction; the qualified appraisal requirements of Section 170(f)(11)(C) and 26 CFR Section 1.170A-17(a) and the sixty-day timing window; the Form 8283 Section B Line 2 digital assets category; and the penalty architecture of Section 6662(e), Section 6662(h), Section 6695A, and the Section 6664(c)(3) reasonable cause condition.

keywords: section 7520 rate charitable lead annuity trust
charitable lead annuity trust vs unitrust

mainEntity.name: Does the short-term capital gain rule apply to a charitable lead trust?

acceptedAnswer.text: Ordinarily no, and the reason is textual. Section 170(e)(1)(A) reduces a contribution of property whose sale would produce gain that is not long-term. But a lead trust contributes an income interest, not the underlying token, and 26 CFR Section 1.170A-4(b)(1) provides that ordinary income property does not include an income interest for which a deduction is allowed under Section 170(f)(2)(B) and Section 1.170A-6(c). Section 1.170A-4(a) likewise limits the reduction to interests described in Section 1.170A-6(b) and Section 1.170A-7(b). The deduction is the Section 7520 present value of the lead interest, computed on fair market value. Confirm the scope with counsel against the specific instrument.

mainEntity.name: How does the Section 7520 rate change a charitable lead trust deduction?

acceptedAnswer.text: It is the discount rate applied to the charity's interest. For a charitable lead annuity trust the interest is a stream of fixed dollars, so a higher rate produces a lower present value, a smaller deduction for a grantor trust, and a larger annuity required to zero out the taxable gift. For a term-of-years charitable lead unitrust the remainder factor depends on the payout rate and the term, so the effect is small and arrives only through the payment-timing adjustment.

mainEntity.name: Which Section 7520 rate applies for an October 2026 funding?

acceptedAnswer.text: The October 2026 Section 7520 rate is 5.6 percent, published in Rev. Rul. 2026-19. Under Section 7520(a) the taxpayer may elect the rate for either of the two months preceding the month in which the valuation date falls, which for an October valuation means September's 5.4 percent under Rev. Rul. 2026-17 or August's 5.2 percent. The election changes the discount rate; it does not change the date as of which the asset is valued.

mainEntity.name: Does a CLUT holding Bitcoin need an annual appraisal?

acceptedAnswer.text: Yes. A charitable lead unitrust pays a fixed percentage of trust value, so the corpus must be revalued every year in order to compute the unitrust amount. That annual figure drives the charity's distribution, the trust's Section 642(c) deduction, and the eventual remainder to the family. A ten-year CLUT funded with digital assets is a recurring appraisal engagement, not a one-time report.

mainEntity.name: Can a charitable lead trust pay its annuity in cryptocurrency?

acceptedAnswer.text: The governing instrument controls, within the requirement that a charitable lead annuity trust pay a guaranteed annuity and a charitable lead unitrust pay a fixed percentage of value. In a non-grantor trust, satisfying the annuity by distributing tokens rather than selling them is a disposition for trust-level gain purposes, so the holding period and adjusted basis of the distributed position determine the character of that gain.

mainEntity.name: Does cryptocurrency qualify for the publicly traded securities exception to the qualified appraisal requirement?

acceptedAnswer.text: No. Digital assets are treated as property under IRS Notice 2014-21, and the practitioner consensus is that exchange-quoted coins do not receive the publicly traded securities shortcut. Above the five thousand dollar threshold in Section 170(f)(11)(C), a qualified appraisal and Form 8283, Section B are required, and the form instructions now list digital assets as a named Section B, Line 2 property category.

mainEntity.name: What happens if the appraisal's valuation date does not match the contribution date?

acceptedAnswer.text: The opinion speaks to the wrong moment. For a volatile asset that is a substantive defect rather than a clerical one. It can support a valuation misstatement penalty under Section 6662(e) while simultaneously undermining the Section 6664(c)(3) reasonable cause defense, which depends on the taxpayer having obtained a qualified appraisal.

mainEntity.name: Does the one-year holding period matter at all in a charitable lead trust?

acceptedAnswer.text: Yes, at the trust level. In a non-grantor CLT a sale within a year of acquisition produces ordinary-rate gain inside the trust; in a grantor CLT that gain flows to the grantor at ordinary rates. The holding period also determines the character of an in-kind distribution made to satisfy the annuity. What it does not do is cap the charitable deduction at adjusted basis, because Section 1.170A-4(b)(1) excludes the lead interest from ordinary income property.

@graph.name: Qualified Digital Asset Appraisal Services
@graph.description: USPAP-compliant qualified appraisals for cryptocurrency, NFT, and digital asset valuation, developed and reported under USPAP Standards 9 and 10, the business and intangible asset appraisal standards. Serving HNW individuals, estate attorneys, CPAs, tax controversy counsel, personal representatives, executors, trust officers, trustees, donors, SDIRA holders and custodians, founders and token holders, and tax professionals requiring IRS-defensible valuations. QDAV scopes engagements by the obligation the report must support, delivers full Appraisal Reports under Standards Rule 10-2(a) wherever a filing obligation introduces intended users beyond the client, applies the three recognized approaches, analyzes restrictions, control, and marketability under Standards Rule 9-4, verifies holdings without custody of private keys, retains contemporaneous market and on-chain evidence in the workfile, and carries a signed certification under Standards Rule 10-3. Reporting packages cover charitable contribution appraisal under IRS Section 170 and Form 8283 Section B, including split-interest funding of charitable lead annuity trusts and charitable lead unitrusts, Section 7520 present value coordination, contribution-date fair market value opinions, recurring annual corpus valuation for charitable lead unitrusts, holding period and adjusted basis evidence, and in-kind distribution support; estate tax valuation for the marital deduction and QTIP elections under Section 2056; date-of-death and alternate valuation date appraisals under Sections 2031 and 2032; gift tax valuation under Section 2512 and Form 709; SDIRA annual value attestation and Form 5498 fair market value support; and examination and litigation support.
